title: What is Microsoft Fabric? (Microsoft Fabric overview)

claims.text: Microsoft Fabric is delivered as a SaaS analytics platform that covers the full data lifecycle — ingestion, transformation, stream processing, warehousing, data science, and BI reporting — inside one product, so teams do not have to stitch together separate Azure services.

Fabric organizes its functionality into role-oriented workloads — Power BI, Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Science, Data Warehouse, Databases, Real-Time Intelligence, Industry Solutions, and the preview Fabric IQ — which all run in the same environment and can share data and items without duplication.

Beneath the workloads sits a shared platform layer of three services used consistently by every experience: OneLake for storage, Copilot for embedded AI assistance, and centralized governance powered by built-in Microsoft Purview.

OneLake is Fabric's single logical data lake, built on Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, and every Fabric compute experience comes preconfigured to use it as its native store — analogous to Office apps automatically using the organization's OneDrive.

Each Fabric tenant gets exactly one OneLake with a single file-system namespace that spans users, regions, and clouds; the tenant maps to the root of the lake and workspaces act like folders beneath it, with lakehouses and other items inside workspaces.

Because Fabric is SaaS, users never deal with Azure infrastructure concepts such as resource groups, RBAC, Azure Resource Manager, redundancy, or region placement, and an Azure account is not required to use the product.

A canonical end-to-end pattern in Fabric is to ingest data with Data Factory, process it with the Data Engineering (Spark) or Real-Time Intelligence workloads, and visualize the result in Power BI — with no manual service integration because all stages share OneLake and the same platform services.

OneLake shortcuts mount existing external storage such as Azure Data Lake Storage, Amazon S3, and Google Cloud Storage as zero-copy references, so cross-cloud data can be analyzed in Fabric without ETL or migration.
When shortcuts target cross-cloud sources, OneLake applies intelligent caching that keeps frequently used data closer to Fabric compute, which both improves locality and reduces cloud egress costs.

Governance in Fabric is centralized in the OneLake Catalog and powered by built-in Purview: permissions, sensitivity labels, and auditing are applied automatically and inherited across Fabric items, and these controls remain enforced even when data is shared across tenant boundaries.

The Real-Time hub is the tenant-wide counterpart of OneLake for data in motion: it catalogs eventstreams, KQL database tables, Microsoft source streams, and Fabric/Azure events so users can discover, ingest, and react to streaming data in one place.

Fabric supports cross-tenant data sharing, letting an organization expose live governed datasets to external Microsoft Entra tenants without copying data; recipients read the data in place and source-side governance policies stay in force.
